text: In October twenty twenty-six, the Atlanta Design Festival wrote down why it was losing money.
The explanation is one sentence, halfway down the second page.
Events cost months before they earn a dollar. The time that goes into building them is the time that would otherwise go into selling.
This is a reading of that claim, against the festival's own records.
Two internal documents. Eighteen slides in September. Six in October.
They agree on the numbers. Tour revenue of fourteen thousand six hundred and eighty-five dollars, seventy percent below peak.
Website traffic down a quarter. A mailing list that has not grown. Eleven months of the year with no money coming in.
The selling year is thirteen weeks long.
Nine of those weeks produce almost nothing. A tenth of the year is in at four weeks out.
Sixty percent arrives in the final week, after every cost has already been paid.
Finding one. The festival cannot forecast, so it cannot commit.
Now the same year, read as a calendar.
Three produced events. A conference, a workshop, and an exhibition. Each one takes months of build.
Against that, the selling calendar. Sponsors are approached in the first quarter. The chapters set their program budgets in the fall.
Put the two on the same axis.
They are the same months.
Finding two. Production does not compete with the festival for money. It competes for January, February and March.
Three consequences follow, and none of them appear in an event budget.
Every product the festival sells is paid, so nobody who does not already know it can enter. The audience cannot grow.
One list, remarketed each year, is the only channel. It has sat flat at about nine thousand four hundred names.
And of six things the festival has to sell, two have ever been sold.
Finding three. The loss on the events is the small number. The large one is the sponsorship and the grants that were never worked.
Two festivals for comparison. Seattle runs a raw, deliberately unglossy program, and raises five figures from a single sponsor.
Portland kept producing. It peaked, and it shut in twenty twenty-one.
The difference is not production value. It is who does the producing.
What the record establishes, and what it does not.
The festival's own figures were never measured. Nobody has priced the months.
Every source here points at the same place on the calendar. The first quarter.
The decision is whether those months go into building events, or into selling the festival.
